newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU Commission takes up arms over BA-American deal.
newsitem.headline: EU Commission takes up arms over BA-American deal.

text.p: Fresh from its successful battle with Boeing Co., the European Commission is seeking concessions from British Airways before it will approve its alliance with AMR Corp.'s American Airlines.

The European Union's antitrust watchdog is reported to have asked the two airlines to give up 350 weekly landing and takoff slots at London's Heathrow Airport, the world's busiest -- nearly double the number suggested by regulators in Britain.
In addition, the commission objects ferociously to the prospect of the airlines getting paid for any of the slots ceded.
On Monday, the Financial Times reported that the commission had told the British government and the two airlines that it was seeking the release of 350 slots at Heathrow.

A spokeswoman for European Transport Commissioner Neil Kinnock, who is reviewing the deal together with EU antitrust chief Karel Van Miert Van Miert, would say only that the commission is currently "looking at possible remedies."

But an EU source said the report was more or less on target, stressing that the commission's position at this stage was a "maximalist" one, designed to secure the best concessions to safeguard competition on the U.S.-British air route.

The commission's antitrust services concluded earlier this year that together the two airlines would control about 60 percent of passenger transportation between Britain and the United States. On 13 trans-Atlantic routes, the deal would eliminate competition altogether, they said.

This view is largely echoed in Washington. The General Accounting Office presented a plan in June under which six U.S. carriers would get 23 daily round trips to Heathrow -- a weekly total of 322 takeoffs and landings.

BA and American plan to coordinate all passenger and cargo arrangements between Europe and the United States, with shared profits and pooled revenue. The proposed deal would involve flight code sharing across the companies' global networks as well as a fully reciprocal frequent flyer programme.

The commission will give its formal approval Wednesday to the planned $16 billion merger between Boeing and McDonnell Douglas Corp. after a long, bitter antitrust investigation that nearly ignited a trade war between the EU and the United States.

Last week, the commission gave its preliminary approval to the merger between the two aerospace giants only after Boeing agreed to a number of provisions aimed at reducing the deal's impact on competition in Europe.
In the past, the European commission has linked its approval of air alliances that would create or strengthen a carrier's dominant position in the market to the release of slots to other airlines.
The commission is unlikely to give its final decision on the BA-American alliance before the fall, possibly in October.
It started its investigation into the BA-American link-up -- as well as Lufthansa's alliance with UAL Corp.'s United Airlines and Dutch airline KLM's with Northwest Airlines Corp. -- in July 1996.
